newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey asks consumers to fund education reforms.
newsitem.headline: Turkey asks consumers to fund education reforms.

text.p: Turkey plans to raise funds from consumers to finance a controversial secularist education plan, according to a bill set to come before parliament this week.
The assembly's planning and budget commission approved on Sunday night a draft clause on contributions to school reforms expected to cost 1,000 trillion lira ($613 million) over the next three years.

Parliament is expected to vote on the draft law this week after rowdy, marathon debates last week on a bill which has drawn fierce opposition from Islamists. They see the reforms as a threat to religious training.
Under the bill, compulsory state schooling will be extended to eight years from five, effectively bringing an end to the primary section of Islamic schools, known as Imam Hatips.
The reform was a key element of military demands for a crackdown on rising religious activism under the Islamist-led government of former prime minister Necmettin Erbakan.
Erbakan resigned under growing secularist pressure in June and was succeeded by a right-left government under Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz.
The budget commission has approved all but one of the bill's 12 articles and is expected to complete its work on Monday, according to parliamentary sources.
They say the draft's fourth article, dealing with religious education and Koran courses, is likely to be withdrawn after facing opposition from a key government ally.

Under the education funding plans, a 10 percent levy is to be imposed on tobacco and alcoholic drinks. Contributions will also come from car registrations, horse racing and football pools gambling, as well as weapons and hunting licenses.

Airline tickets, television advertising fees and mobile phone subscriptions, along with tax and custom declarations will also be subject to the funding plans. Some bourse transactions will also contribute to the education reforms.

Finance Minister Zekeriya Temizel told commission members 72 trillion lira ($44 million) was needed by the end of 1997 for the schooling plan. He said part of this would come from the budget and said talks had begun with the World Bank on raising credit.
